name: Tea tree oil

lead: Tea tree oil is the essential oil distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves, used in soaps, washes, gels and shampoos for acne, post-shave breakouts, body odor, scalp care and eyelid cleansing, aiming at clearer skin and a healthier scalp.

Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, disrupts bacterial and yeast membranes in lab studies and suppresses inflammatory mediators in human monocytes. Human evidence includes small pilot trials, such as a 5% acne gel pilot with 18 people, and eyelid-mite studies. Claims of lowering testosterone and helping shaving rest on anecdote.

paras: It is used diluted, as a spot treatment, in a wash or shampoo or a premixed gel, applied topically. Skin changes show over weeks of regular use.
Irritation and allergic contact dermatitis are documented, with reactions in a small percentage of users, and swallowing is toxic. Labels advise external use only, and pure oil is generally diluted.

angle.text: Tea tree oil's antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory action means fewer breakouts and less odor, for clearer skin and a healthier scalp. Small trials exist for acne and eyelid mites; the testosterone and shaving claims are anecdotal.

lead: Tea tree oil is the essential oil steam-distilled from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a tree native to eastern Australia, and its main component is terpinen-4-ol.[1][2] It is one of the most widely sold botanical skin-care ingredients: it appears in face washes, spot gels, body soaps, anti-dandruff shampoos, foot products and shave products, and some people use the neat oil, diluted, as a home treatment for blemishes.[3][2][4]

People use it to look better mainly by treating the things that interfere with clear, calm skin and a clean scalp: breakouts, flaking from dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis, and irritation after shaving. The chain is antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory action in the skin, then fewer inflamed spots or less scaling, then a clearer complexion or scalp.[5][6][7][8][9]

Research includes laboratory studies of its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity, a 1990 randomized trial of a 5 percent gel in acne in 124 people, a 2002 randomized trial of a 5 percent shampoo in dandruff in 126 people, and studies of eyelid Demodex mites.[5][6][7][8][9][10] The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says a small amount of research suggests it might help acne.[4] Contact allergy, a 2007 case series linking tea tree and lavender oils to breast enlargement in three prepubertal boys, and poisoning when swallowed are documented.[11][9][2][4]
Tea tree oil has a history of nearly a century of commercial use in Australia, beginning with chemist Arthur Penfold's work on the oil's antiseptic properties in the 1920s.[5][2][12]
infobox: Topical (gel, soap, wash, shampoo); not for swallowing[4]
From the 1920s, after Arthur Penfold's work[2][12]
Acne, dandruff, post-shave skin, foot and body products
Not an approved drug in the US; complementary medicine in Australia[2]
5% gel vs benzoyl peroxide in acne (1990); 5% shampoo in dandruff (2002)[8][9]

paras: Tea tree oil is sold for skin and scalp care, and the most common appearance goals are clearer skin, less dandruff and fewer shaving bumps. Consumer products range from 5 to 10 percent gels and washes to the neat oil, which labels advise diluting for skin use.[2][4]

A US label for a tea tree oil antifungal soap lists use against athlete's foot, jock itch and ringworm, and says it helps reduce body odor, acne, itching and eczema from fungi [3]. A systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included tea tree oil among botanicals searched [13].
One T Nation user describes making a shave gel from tea tree oil, witch hazel and aloe to avoid post-shave breakouts [14].

Wikipedia reports that the oil is promoted for dandruff, acne, lice, herpes, insect bites, scabies and skin fungal or bacterial infections, but that few studies support these claims; a 2015 Cochrane review found one low-quality trial showing benefit for acne lesions compared with placebo.[2] NCCIH states that a small amount of research suggests it might help acne and athlete's foot, though for athlete's foot it may not work as well as standard treatments, and that there are too few studies on nail fungus to draw conclusions.[4]

Tea tree oil is promoted as a natural acne treatment, usually as a gel or spot product. In a 1990 single-blind randomized trial in the Medical Journal of Australia, 124 people with mild to moderate acne used either a 5 percent tea tree oil gel or a 5 percent benzoyl peroxide lotion. Both reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesions, the tea tree oil acted more slowly, and fewer side effects were reported with tea tree oil.[9] The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says a small amount of research suggests tea tree oil might help acne.[4] A registered phase II pilot of a tea tree oil gel for facial acne enrolled 18 participants.[15] A 2015 Cochrane review of acne treatments, as summarised by Wikipedia, found one low-quality trial showing benefit over placebo.[2]

Shampoos containing 5 percent tea tree oil are sold for dandruff, and the scalp is a common looksmaxxing concern because flakes show on dark hair and clothing. In a randomized single-blind trial published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in 2002, 126 people aged 14 and over washed daily for four weeks with either a 5 percent tea tree oil shampoo or a placebo shampoo. A scalp lesion score fell from 91.0 to 53.0 with tea tree oil, compared with 99.7 to 88.2 with placebo, and patient-reported itchiness improved by 23 percent versus 12 percent.[8] A commentary in American Family Physician noted that only one participant in each group was completely free of dandruff at four weeks, that the oil's odor may have let participants guess their group, and that no serious adverse events were reported.[8] A comprehensive review of seborrheic dermatitis lists tea tree oil among alternative therapies.[16] A 2024 review of natural options for hair loss includes tea tree oil among the herbal ingredients it discusses, alongside rosemary and peppermint oils.[17]

On T Nation one user describes mixing tea tree oil with witch hazel and aloe as a homemade shave gel after years of breakouts from shaving.[14] No trial has tested tea tree oil for razor bumps or ingrown hairs. Product labels for tea tree oil soaps also list reducing body odor and itching.[3]

Tea tree oil has been studied for eyelid Demodex infestation and blepharitis, including 5% tea tree oil as a comparator to intense pulsed light, an eye gel trial in anterior blepharitis and eyelid cleansers [10][18][19][20][21][22]. Other studies and registrations cover MRSA decolonization body wash, hand-hygiene soap, nasal use in dialysis patients, burns, nipple cracks and dental or periodontal applications [23][24][25][26][27][28][29][30].

The oil is defined by the international standard ISO 4730, in which terpinen-4-ol makes up about 35 to 48 percent, gamma-terpinene 14 to 28 percent, alpha-terpinene 6 to 12 percent, and 1,8-cineole up to 10 percent; terpinen-4-ol, gamma-terpinene and alpha-terpinene together are roughly 70 to 90 percent of the oil. It is pale yellow to nearly colourless with a camphor-like smell, and its composition changes as it oxidises in air.[2]

The source plant, Melaleuca alternifolia, is a tree or tall shrub of the myrtle family that grows to about 7 metres with papery bark and narrow, oil-rich leaves. It was described botanically in 1905 by Joseph Maiden and Ernst Betche and raised to species rank by Edwin Cheel in 1925. It is endemic to Australia, from the Grafton district of New South Wales to Maryborough in Queensland, often growing along streams and swampy ground.[31] Large plantations appeared in the 1970s and 1980s, mostly in New South Wales, and other Melaleuca species are now also grown in countries such as Tunisia, Egypt, Malaysia, Vietnam and the US.[2]

Indigenous Australians of eastern inland areas inhaled oil from crushed leaves for coughs and colds, laid leaves on wounds under a poultice and made leaf infusions for sore throats and skin ailments, according to Wikipedia; NCCIH likewise notes traditional use of the leaves on wounds, burns and insect bites.[31][4] The name 'tea tree' is generally attributed to Captain James Cook's description of a shrub brewed as a tea substitute.[2]

Commercial production began in the 1920s after Australian chemist Arthur Penfold reported the oil's antiseptic properties.[2] Penfold (1890-1980) was a research chemist who joined the Technological Museum in Sydney in 1919, published about a hundred papers on Australian plant oils, and in the 1920s proposed commercial production of tea tree oil on the basis of its antiseptic properties; he later became the museum's director.[12] During World War II tea tree oil was used to treat skin lesions in munitions factory workers.[2] Plantation production expanded from the 1970s, and by 2006 a Clinical Microbiology Reviews article could describe nearly a century of use in Australia and worldwide sales as neat oil and in many products.[2][5]

In laboratory studies, exposure to tea tree oil damaged cell membranes of Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus and Candida albicans [6], and time-kill and leakage assays on S. aureus attributed activity to components including terpinen-4-ol, 1,8-cineole and alpha-terpineol [32][33]. Terpinen-4-ol suppressed production of TNF-alpha, interleukins and prostaglandin E2 by activated human monocytes [7]. Antifungal activity of its components has also been reported [34].
A 2007 study using human cell lines found that lavender and tea tree oils showed estrogen-like and anti-androgen activity, the basis for the endocrine questions described under adverse effects.[9]

The two best-known human trials on appearance outcomes are the 1990 acne trial (124 participants, 5 percent gel versus 5 percent benzoyl peroxide lotion; both reduced lesions, with tea tree oil slower and with fewer side effects) and the 2002 dandruff trial (126 participants, 5 percent shampoo versus placebo; scalp lesion score fell by about 42 percent versus about 12 percent).[9][8]

A registered phase II pilot of tea tree oil gel for facial acne enrolled 18 participants [15]; an encyclopedic summary states that 5% gels have shown efficacy comparable to benzoyl peroxide, though the published literature do not include the underlying trial data [1].

In ophthalmology, a randomized study of 40 patients compared intense pulsed light with 5% tea tree oil as the control for ocular demodicosis [10]. An open-label trial compared tea tree oil eye gel with standard treatment in anterior blepharitis [18]. A randomized crossover study of five commercial anti-demodectic eyelid cleansers assessed short-term tolerability in 30 healthy people [19]. Registered trials involve chronic blepharitis (n=34), ocular demodicosis (n=60) and dry eye compared with azithromycin (n=50) [20][21][22].

A protocol for a randomized trial of 5% tea tree oil body wash against standard body wash to prevent MRSA colonization in critically ill adults has been published [23]. A randomized trial examined a tea tree oil soap for hand hygiene [24]. Small registered studies cover burns (n=30), nipple cracks (n=90) and gum disease [26][27][29][28].
Wikipedia reports limited evidence for eyelid crusting caused by Demodex mites and says the oil is not recommended for nail fungus or for head lice in children.[2]
The published literature contain no large randomized trial of tea tree oil for facial appearance, wrinkles or hair growth.
A review of tea tree oil in the Cutis dermatology literature and a 2012 Dermatitis entry on the oil discuss tolerability and contact allergy alongside its uses.[35][11]

A dermatology reference on tea tree oil covers allergic contact dermatitis [11], and a 2005 review in Cutis discusses its use and tolerability [35]. An encyclopedic summary reports that diluted tea tree oil is generally well tolerated, with irritation, dryness or allergic contact dermatitis in a small percentage of users, and that undiluted use can cause severe irritation and ingestion can be toxic [1]. That summary is AI-generated. Product labelling advises external use only [3]. A 2006 review notes that the toxicity of the oil is discussed briefly in the literature [5].

Wikipedia describes tea tree oil as highly toxic if swallowed, to be kept away from children and pets, and says irritation and allergic contact dermatitis risk rises as the oil oxidises.[2] NCCIH says it should not be swallowed, as ingestion has caused confusion, unsteadiness, inability to walk and coma, and that most people can use topical products without problems, with redness or irritation more likely if a product is old or exposed to heat, light or air.[4] Wikipedia also reports a possible risk of breast enlargement in men and prepubertal children, and that a 2018 NIEHS study found four constituents to be endocrine disruptors; it also reports that topical use at high doses has caused toxicity or death in dogs and cats, and that tea tree oil accounted for 17 percent of 749 essential oil poisoning cases in New South Wales from 2014 to 2018.[2]

In a case series in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2007, three prepubertal boys aged 4, 7 and 10 with normal steroid levels developed breast enlargement while using products containing lavender and tea tree oils, and it resolved after the products were stopped. Laboratory experiments showed estrogen-like and anti-androgen effects for both oils, and the authors concluded that repeated skin exposure probably caused the condition in these boys.[9] The report involved three children and does not establish how common the effect is.[9]

Contact allergy is the most frequently described skin reaction, and reports say the risk increases as the oil oxidises with exposure to air, heat and light; the Wikipedia summary also reports that reactions are noted to decrease as eucalyptol content falls.[2][4] Wikipedia reports 749 poisoning cases involving essential oils in New South Wales from 2014 to 2018, 17 percent of which involved tea tree oil, mostly in children, and that high-dose topical application has caused toxicity in dogs and cats.[2] Wikipedia's entry on the plant notes that as of 2006 no deaths had been reported in the medical literature.[31]

In the US it is not an approved drug, though it appears in skin care products. In Australia it is approved as a complementary medicine for aromatherapy. The EU's herbal medicines committee recognises traditional use for minor wounds, insect bites and small boils, and says products should not be used by people under 12.[2]

NCCIH advises talking with a health care provider about complementary health approaches and notes topical tea tree oil products may be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding, while the oil should not be swallowed.[4] Product labels typically advise external use only and keeping products away from the eyes.[3]

Tea tree oil appears in looksmaxxing and fitness communities as a skin-care and shaving ingredient rather than as a headline compound. On T Nation, one user credits a homemade shave gel containing it with ending post-shave breakouts.[14] Another poster stated that research suggests lavender and tea tree oils lower testosterone; no study of this in adult men has been published, although the 2007 case series examined estrogen-like and anti-androgen activity in cell lines and in boys.[36][9]

Mentions of the oil in hair-growth discussion typically place it alongside rosemary and peppermint oils; a 2024 review of natural alternatives for androgenetic alopecia covers these botanicals and notes that finasteride and minoxidil are the only FDA-approved treatments for the condition.[17]

lore.intro: Community material on tea tree oil is mostly about skin, scalp and shaving use, with occasional hormone claims on T Nation.[14][36] Believers treat it as a natural antimicrobial for breakouts and flakes; researchers describe trials of 5 percent products plus documented allergy and endocrine questions.
